findings.title: CT-5's "commit subject is T-n" condition never fails, so TC-10 and TC-18 expect behaviour CT-5 doesn't have
quotes: the commit's subject is `T-n: <title>`
and a variant where a commit `fix up` (no `T-n:` subject) follows `T-2: Two`
The commits named `T-n: ...` for a task of the epic, newest first.
commit, base = commits[0], parent_of(root, commits[-1])
findings.fix: drop the subject condition from CT-5 and say the commit is `commits_of(...)[0]`, a task commit by construction. Remove TC-10's `fix up` variant, or have CT-5 compare against HEAD if a later non-task commit should stop reuse. Make TC-18's `T-3` a task of E-1 so the test really covers "another commit".

sources.situation: `collect` always picks its commit from `evidence.commits_of`, which keeps only `T-n:` commits of the epic's tasks. So the commit `reused_suite` gets always has a `T-n:` subject. In TC-10's `fix up` variant, evidence still checks out `T-2: Two`, the history there still ends with T-2's passing review, and CT-5 reuses it. TC-10 asserts "no `reused` key". TC-18 has the same problem when `T-3: Three` isn't a task of E-1: `commits_of` skips it and CT-5 reuses T-2's review. CT-5's guard against "another commit" really comes from `commits_of`, not from the subject check.

`collect` takes `commit = commits_of(...)[0]`, which skips non-`T-n` subjects. With a `fix up` commit on top, evidence still runs at the `T-2: Two` commit, whose subject and history meet every CT-5 condition. A faithful CT-5 implementation therefore reuses, and TC-10 fails. To make it pass, a builder would add an undeclared HEAD check. TC-18 has the same trap: unless `T-3: Three` is added to tasks.md as a done E-1 task, `commits_of` ignores it, T-2's review is reused, and the test fails for fixture reasons rather than catching the "older review" bug it names.

findings.reason: `commits_of` (evidence.py:138-152) keeps only `T-n:` commits of the epic's tasks, and `collect` takes `commits[0]`. The subject condition in CT-5 therefore always holds. In TC-10's `fix up` variant evidence still picks `T-2: Two` and CT-5 reuses its review, so the "no `reused` key" assertion contradicts CT-5. TC-18's `T-3: Three` is not a task in tasks.md, so `commits_of` skips it and T-2's review is reused.
findings.note: CT-5: the commit is commits_of(...)[0], a task commit by construction; dropped TC-10's fix-up variant; TC-18's T-3 is a task of E-1

findings.title: US-3 is built before the CT-4 field it relies on
quotes: ### US-3 Jury evidence reuses suite results
- Delivers: CT-4
`suite.command` equal to `tests.suite` and `suite.code` 0
run evidence at a commit whose epic-close review ran the suite on a clean tree
findings.fix: move CT-4 and TC-20 into US-3 (or put US-5 before US-3). Leave US-5 with TC-16 and QS-style proof of the fix-check round.

sources.situation: CT-5, delivered by US-3, reuses a suite only when the review line holds `suite.command` and `suite.code`. Today `implement.review` writes no `suite` key; CT-4 adds it, and CT-4 comes later in US-5. When US-3 is done, its own independent test can't be shown in a real flow: no review has a `suite` key yet, so nothing is ever reused. Only TC-9's hand-written history line passes. US-5 then delivers only CT-4, while its own requirement FR-13 is delivered by CT-5 in US-3.

findings.reason: US-3 delivers CT-5, which reads `suite.command` and `suite.code` from the review line. `implement.review` writes no `suite` key today, and CT-4, which adds it, is in US-5, later in the build order. US-3 also lists TC-9 as covering CT-4 (tests.md) although it does not deliver CT-4. Only TC-9's hand-written history makes the US-3 tests pass.
findings.note: Build order: US-5 delivers CT-4 (TC-20) before US-3 delivers CT-5 (TC-16 moved to US-3)

findings.title: Running test_flow's CLI calls in-process can import fastembed, breaking test_nfr2_offline's check
quotes: assert "fastembed" not in sys.modules
`tests/test_flow.py:cli` and `tests/test_implement.py:nio` (existing) call it instead of `subprocess.run`
with the CLI in-process, its 145 loads were the largest remaining cost of test_implement.py (RF-11)
findings.fix: in CT-1, either keep `sys.modules` clean (snapshot and restore which `fastembed` modules are loaded, in the `finally`), or change `test_nfr2_offline` to check in a fresh subprocess that the commands don't import fastembed. Add a TC for it.

sources.situation: The plan says the CLI loads the embedding model on many commands. Once `cli` calls `main()` in the test process, any earlier test_flow test whose CLI command embeds leaves `fastembed` in the shared `sys.modules`. `test_flow.py` runs every `test_*` in one process (`for name, test in list(globals().items())`), so `test_nfr2_offline` can then fail depending on test order. Until now that check only held because every `cli` call ran in its own process. TC-4 reads only the test's own source, so it would not catch this.

findings.reason: `index.embed` imports fastembed lazily (index.py:48), and only `query`, `index` and `pack` reach it (query.py, cli.py:343). The `cli` helper in test_flow.py only runs `nio flow ...`, and flow commands never call `embed`. `test_nfr2_offline` runs in the test_flow process, and the `nio(...)` helper CT-1 doesn't convert stays a subprocess. So going in-process cannot put fastembed into that process's `sys.modules`.

findings.title: CT-1 leaves out test_flow.py's own `nio` subprocess helper
quotes: def nio(root, *args):
`tests/test_flow.py:cli` and `tests/test_implement.py:nio` (existing) call it instead of `subprocess.run`
findings.fix: list `tests/test_flow.py:nio` among CT-1's callers; it can become `return run_main(root, *args)`. Or say why it stays a subprocess (FR-2).

sources.situation: `tests/test_flow.py` has a second CLI helper, `nio` at line 1517. It runs `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "from nio.cli import main; main()", *args], ...)` and already returns `(code, stdout, stderr)`, the exact shape of `run_main`. CT-1 doesn't mention it, so it keeps starting a process for each call while the two helpers it lists change.

findings.note: CT-1 says why tests/test_flow.py:nio stays a subprocess (keeps fastembed out of test_flow's process)

findings.title: TC-6 can't see whether a signal-killed file stops xargs, because all its files start in one batch
quotes: Setup: `suite_dir` with `test_a.py` printing `A RAN`; `test_b.py` `assert 1 == 2, "B FAILED"`; `test_c.py` killing itself with `os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGKILL)`; `test_d.py` `raise SystemExit("D FAILED")`; `test_z.py` printing `Z RAN`.
`|| exit 1` turns a file killed by a signal into exit 1, so `xargs` goes on with the other files (research RF-12).
findings.fix: give TC-6 more than eight files, with the killed and failing files first in sort order and a passing file ninth or later. Assert that the later file's marker is in the output.

sources.situation: with `xargs -P8` and only 5 files (8 in TC-17), every file is launched before any fails. If `|| exit 1` is dropped, or a file's exit maps to 255, xargs stops launching new files, but no file is left to launch. `Z RAN` still appears, and the exit is still non-zero. The FR-3 "each file to its end even when another failed" bug passes both tests.

findings.reason: TC-6 has 5 files and `xargs -P8` starts all of them at once, so no file is left to launch after the killed or failing one. `Z RAN` appears and the exit is non-zero even if `|| exit 1` is dropped. The FR-3/AC-6 clause "after running every other file" is not tested.
findings.note: TC-6: ten files, the killed and failing ones first, a tenth that starts only once a slot frees

findings.title: TC-5 is a wall-clock test inside the parallel suite, which the plan itself says would fail under load
quotes: Assert: the suite exits 0, and its wall-clock is at most 1.5 times the single file's.
a timing test inside the suite would fail under load [agent]
findings.fix: widen the margin, for example sleeps of 5 s and a bound of `<= single + 3 s`. Or gate TC-5 behind an env var and leave the ratio to QS-1, as NFR-1 already is.

sources.situation: TC-5 lives in tests/test_implement.py, which the new suite runs alongside seven other files. TC-5 then starts eight concurrent `uv run` processes while those run. The 1.5x bound (about 3 s against about 2 s plus uv startup) can trip from contention alone, so every epic-close review and every evidence run can fail without any real regression.

findings.reason: TC-5 is in tests/test_implement.py, which the new suite runs, and it asserts a 1.5x wall-clock bound on eight concurrent `uv run` processes. The plan's own decision says "a timing test inside the suite would fail under load". Under contention from the other files it can fail with no regression.
findings.note: TC-5: 4 s sleeps, so queueing shows as 8 s or more against a 1.5x bound

findings.title: TC-3's flow.lock assertion can never fail
quotes: then with `flow.next_step` replaced by a function that sets `os.environ["NIO_LEAK"] = "1"`, calls `os.chdir("/")` and raises `RuntimeError("boom")`
extra = ["--by", BY] if by and args and args[0] in ("start", "done", "park", "abandon", "seen") else []
findings.fix: make the raising call a writing command that takes the lock and fails inside it, for example `run_main(root, "flow", "park", S, "x", "--by", BY)` with `flow.record` raising. Then assert that no `flow.lock` remains and that a second `park` succeeds.

sources.situation: all three calls are `flow next` without `--by`, so no lock is taken, and the raising call is a stub that never locks. "no `flow.lock` file exists" holds no matter what `run_main` does, so the AC-3 clause "no flow lock it took is left behind" is not tested.

findings.note: TC-3: the failing call is a park that takes the lock and fails inside it; asserts no lock and a second park succeeds

findings.title: TC-20's "doesn't close its epic" half has no such task in its setup
quotes: Setup: `impl()` with one epic of one task in direct mode
a review of a task that doesn't close its epic has no `suite` key
findings.fix: use an epic of two tasks and assert that the first task's review line has no `suite` key.

sources.situation: with one task, every review closes the epic, so the second assertion has nothing to check. A `review` that always writes `suite: {"command": ..., "code": null}` breaks CT-4's "the key is absent otherwise" and passes.

findings.note: TC-20: two tasks; the first review has no suite key
